title: What they share
hook: the creeds, baptism, the Lord's Prayer, and one Lord; many now pray together

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was charismata, from a dusty room on Azusa Street. Your line was come, holy spirit.

On a hill in the French countryside sits a village called Taizé. Young people arrive from all over the world with backpacks and sleeping bags: Catholics, Lutherans, Orthodox, Anglicans, Pentecostals, people with no church at all. Three times a day a bell rings, and everyone walks into a long, low, candlelit church and sits on the floor. They sing short, simple songs, over and over, in many languages. Then a long silence, together. Nobody asks which church you belong to. Brother Roger, a young Swiss man who took in refugees during the war, started it in 1940. After two weeks of splits, today's word is the long work of coming back together.
screen: `A VILLAGE CALLED TAIZÉ.` → `EVERY CHURCH, ON ONE FLOOR.` → `SINGING, THEN SILENCE.`

segments.voice: Ecumenism comes from the Greek oikoumene, the whole inhabited world. The early church's councils were called ecumenical because they gathered bishops from everywhere. Now it means the movement to heal divisions between churches. Its heart is a prayer Jesus prays in John's Gospel, the night before he dies: "That they all may be one; as thou, Father, art in me, and I in thee." For long stretches, the churches didn't pray that together. In the twentieth century, that began to change. A missionary conference in Edinburgh in 1910 found that division confused the very people they hoped to reach. The World Council of Churches, founded in 1948, now brings together Orthodox, Anglican and Protestant churches worldwide. The Catholic Church isn't a member, but since the Second Vatican Council it has worked closely alongside, calling other Christians separated brothers and sisters. Many evangelical and Pentecostal churches keep their distance from formal bodies, but pray with other Christians in their own ways. The differences are real, and nobody pretends otherwise: communion, authority, ministry. But much is shared. The Bible. The Nicene Creed, said in many churches. The Lord's Prayer. Baptism in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, which many churches now recognize in each other. And one Lord. Every January there's a Week of Prayer for Christian Unity. Now look back: one church, then many; the councils; the ancient churches of the east; the Church of the East; 1054; the Orthodox; the Catholics; the Reformation; Lutherans and the Reformed; Anglicans; Anabaptists; Baptists; Methodists; Pentecostals. Fifteen days, one family.
screen: `OIKOUMENE: THE WHOLE WORLD.` · `EDINBURGH 1910, GENEVA 1948.` · `THE DIFFERENCES ARE REAL.` · `ONE CREED, ONE PRAYER, ONE LORD.` · then, large: `THAT THEY ALL MAY BE ONE.`

segments.voice: If you pray, say the Lord's Prayer slowly, all the way through, Our Father which art in heaven, Hallowed be thy name, picturing a Coptic church, an Orthodox one, a Catholic one, a Baptist one and a little Pentecostal storefront, all saying it with you. If you don't pray, just picture them all, saying the same words in many languages.
Ecumenism. From the Greek for the whole inhabited world: the work of healing the divisions between churches.
Your line: that they may be one. Many churches, one prayer. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Many churches keep the Week of Prayer for Christian Unity each January, often with services where members of different churches pray together, and many young Christians travel to Taizé to worship side by side.

notes: Editor review (282-299 pass): cut 'every week of the year, thousands', 'ten minutes' of silence, 'hundreds of churches', 'said by most churches' and 'in every church there is' (Quakers, for one, keep no set prayers); the 'Lord's Prayer is said in every church' myth replaced; fork's Taizé placed near the line dividing occupied France (it lay in the unoccupied zone).
Taizé: founded by Brother Roger Schutz in 1940; he sheltered refugees, including Jewish refugees, until 1942. Prayer three times a day; silence of several minutes. Confirm details.
WCC: founded in Amsterdam, 1948, headquartered in Geneva; about 350 member churches. The Catholic Church is not a member but participates (e.g. in Faith and Order).
'Separated brethren' language from Vatican II rendered as 'separated brothers and sisters'. Confirm.
Mutual recognition of baptism: many but not all churches (e.g. some Baptist churches practice believers' baptism and may not recognize infant baptism). Script says 'many'.
